All 4 tests pass. Summary of what was built and one important scientific finding along the way:

## Files

**`/workspace/sir_network.py`** — builds `nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n=2000, p=8/1999, seed=10)` (mean degree ≈ 8) and runs discrete-time SIR: random index case per run, per-neighbor infection attempts with probability `T` at each transmission step, recovery exactly 3 steps after infection.

**`/workspace/test_sir_network.py`** — pytest suite (run with `/opt/venv/bin/python -m pytest`, since the system python lacks networkx):

```
T=0.05 subcritical:  mean final size    4.98  ( 0.25% of n), 50 runs in 0.001s
T=0.25 supercritical: mean final size 1774.98  (88.75% of n), 50 runs in 0.094s
single run worst case: 1.76 ms   → all assertions pass with wide margins
```

## The caveat you asked me to note (and why iteration was needed)

My first implementation gave each node **3 full transmission rounds**, and the subcritical assertion failed (mean ≈ 130 ≈ 6.5% of n, with ~11/50 runs taking off). I verified the simulator against ground truth: bond-percolating the graph with per-edge probability `1-(1-T)^3` produces a largest cluster of exactly 639 nodes, matching the big runs. So with 3 full rounds, `R0_eff = [1-(1-T)^3]·8 ≈ 1.14 > 1` — T=0.05 is genuinely marginally supercritical, because the naive predictor `R0 = T·k·3 = 1.2` double-counts correlated repeat attempts at the same neighbor.

The fix (documented in the module docstring): *"recovers after exactly 3 steps"* is implemented as a 3-step lifespan **counting the exposure step** — infected during step t, attempts at t+1 and t+2, recovered at t+3. That gives `R0_eff ≈ 0.78 < 1` at T=0.05 and `≈ 3.5` at T=0.25, matching your stated regime classification. Both conventions are spelled out in the code so the choice is auditable; if you intended 3 full action rounds instead, no simulation can put T=0.05 below 2% of n — that threshold is physically unreachable there.
